sections.title: Overview
blocks: ‘Red leg’ is a presentation, not a diagnosis. Up to a third of patients admitted with ‘cellulitis’ turn out to have a **mimic** (pseudocellulitis). This page brings together the Module 5 red-leg teaching and the referral triggers for leg ulcers.

Calf swelling and tenderness, less skin redness
Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, toxic

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: Compare the photos below. Venous eczema is scaly and itchy on **both** legs. Lipodermatosclerosis is indurated and tapering. True cellulitis is hot, tender, **one-sided** and expanding.

ul: Ask: **one leg or two?** Acute or chronic? Fever or rigors? Itch or pain? Is there a portal of entry?
Mark the border and record observations (NEWS2).
Wells score with D-dimer or Doppler if DVT is possible.
Check pulses or ABPI if there is an ulcer, or before compression.

ddx.name: Venous eczema / stasis dermatitis
ddx.f: Bilateral or chronic, itchy, scale, haemosiderin, no fever

ddx.name: Acute lipodermatosclerosis
ddx.f: Painful, woody, red skin above the ankle, often misdiagnosed as cellulitis

ddx.name: DVT
ddx.f: Calf pain and swelling, less intense redness

ddx.name: Contact dermatitis (e.g. to dressings)
ddx.f: Itchy, vesicular, matches the area covered

ddx.name: Necrotising fasciitis
ddx.f: **Severe pain out of proportion**, rapid progression, systemic toxicity. **ED**

ddx.name: Pyoderma gangrenosum / vasculitis
ddx.f: Ulcer edge features, purpura, systemic disease

refer.t: Pain out of proportion, purple bullae, crepitus, or a rapidly spreading area: **necrotising fasciitis**.
Sepsis signs: low blood pressure, tachycardia, confusion, mottling.
A cold, pulseless or ischaemic limb.
A diabetic foot that is hot, red or ulcerated.

head: Situation
Action
rows: Facial or orbital cellulitis, or rapidly spreading
Critical limb ischaemia, rest pain or gangrene
Leg ulcer not improving, or atypical edge
Tissue viability plus dermatology or vascular
Red leg with no fever, bilateral, chronic and itchy
Rethink: venous eczema. Emollient, topical steroid and compression, **no antibiotic**
Treat portals of entry; discuss prophylaxis with a clinician

pearls: Venous eczema responds to emollient plus a topical steroid and compression (after ABPI). Antibiotics do nothing for it.
Recurrent ‘cellulitis’ in the same leg may be lipodermatosclerosis. Look at the whole leg history.
